final_proof:
There is a terminological slip in the statement: although it calls \(f\wedge g\) the “pointwise maximum,” the displayed definition defines it using \(\min\). Thus the claim concerns the pointwise minimum, and that is what we prove.

Let
\[
h=\frac12\bigl(f+g-|f-g|\bigr).
\]
We prove that \(f\wedge g=h\) by equality of functions. Fix an arbitrary \(s\in S\), and put \(x=f(s)\) and \(y=g(s)\). By the definitions of the pointwise operations,
\[
h(s)=\frac12\bigl(x+y-|x-y|\bigr).
\]
Because the usual order on \(\mathbb R\) is total, either \(x\le y\) or \(y\le x\).

If \(x\le y\), then \(x-y\le0\), so \(|x-y|=-(x-y)=y-x\). Hence
\[
h(s)=\frac12\bigl(x+y-(y-x)\bigr)=\frac12(2x)=x=\min\{x,y\}.
\]

If \(y\le x\), then \(x-y\ge0\), so \(|x-y|=x-y\). Hence
\[
h(s)=\frac12\bigl(x+y-(x-y)\bigr)=\frac12(2y)=y=\min\{x,y\}.
\]
Thus in every case
\[
h(s)=\min\{f(s),g(s)\}=(f\wedge g)(s).
\]
Since \(s\in S\) was arbitrary, the two functions agree at every element of \(S\), and therefore, by function extensionality,
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle f\wedge g=\frac12\bigl(f+g-|f-g|\bigr)}.
\]
If \(S=\varnothing\), the same conclusion follows because the two functions from \(S\) to \(\mathbb R\) agree vacuously at every element of \(S\).
